text.title: Incident Comms Templates Internal External Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules every incident comms template bundle MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The bundle MUST contain the four templates (status-page update, customer email, exec brief, internal channel post) and one severity x audience matrix that maps every severity level from the org's incident runbook to the audiences that receive a message. A template MUST NOT be sent to an audience the matrix does not list for that severity; the highest severity always includes the public status page.

rationale.source: Atlassian Incident Management Handbook (incident communication); PagerDuty Incident Response documentation

rule.rationale: Without the matrix, the decision "do we email customers?" is made at 03:00 by whoever is on call, and it goes both ways: a P3 internal degradation triggers a 40,000-recipient apology, or a P1 goes unannounced because nobody felt authorised. The matrix moves that decision to daylight.

rule.statement: Each external template carries a numeric first-post deadline measured from incident declaration and an update interval, both set per severity in the matrix. Every update ends with "next update by <time with timezone>". A promised interval that passes with no change is itself an update ("no change, still investigating"), never silence.

rationale.source: Atlassian Statuspage guidance on incident updates; Google SRE book (Beyer et al., 2016), ch. 14 Managing Incidents

rule.rationale: Silence during an outage is read as abandonment. Customers refresh the page, then open tickets, then post publicly, and the support queue becomes a second incident. A "no change" post at the promised minute keeps the queue flat and buys the responders the time they need.

rule.statement: The status-page template uses the four lifecycle states in order: Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, Resolved. Every update carries the current state, a timestamp with timezone, the impact (which components, regions or customer segments, and what they cannot do), and the next-update time. Component status set on the page MUST agree with the text of the update.

rationale.source: Atlassian Statuspage documentation (incident statuses and component status)

rule.rationale: A page that says "Operational" next to an update that says "checkout failing for EU customers" teaches every reader that the page lies. The four states are the vocabulary status-page consumers and integrations already parse; inventing a fifth one ("Partially fixed") breaks subscribers' filters and their trust at the same time.

rule.statement: Customer-facing templates (status page, customer email) MUST NOT contain an unconfirmed root cause, blame directed at a person, team or vendor, internal system or host names, or any customer name or personal data. Cause appears only in the Resolved message or the post-incident report, after it is confirmed.

rationale.source: PagerDuty Incident Response documentation (external communications); Google SRE book ch. 14

rule.rationale: "We believe the database cluster is the cause" becomes a quote in a customer's own incident review, and retracting it two hours later costs more trust than "we are investigating" ever would. Naming a vendor draws them into a public dispute mid-incident; naming a host leaks architecture to anyone reading the page.

rule.statement: The internal channel template MUST carry: severity, incident commander (a named person), communications lead, blast radius, current hypothesis, actions in flight each with an owner, link to the incident channel or document, and the next checkpoint time. Hypotheses and system names belong here and nowhere external.

rationale.source: Google SRE book ch. 14 Managing Incidents (incident commander, communications lead roles)

rule.rationale: The internal post is where a responder joining at minute 40 learns who is in charge and what not to duplicate. Without a named commander two engineers restart the same service; without a comms lead the CTO posts on the status page from a hallway conversation. The internal template is also the only place a hypothesis is allowed, which is what keeps it out of the customer email.

rule.statement: The exec brief fits on one screen without scrolling and has exactly five fields: customer impact in business terms (customers affected, revenue at risk, SLA credits exposed), ETA or "unknown, next update at <time>", decisions needed from the reader, what is being done, next update time. Technical narrative is forbidden in the brief.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in incident management; Atlassian Incident Management Handbook

rule.rationale: An executive reads the brief on a phone between meetings and needs to know one thing: is there a decision only they can make (spend, customer call, press line). Three paragraphs about connection pools produce a reply-all asking "so is it fixed?", which the commander now has to answer instead of running the incident.

rule.statement: The Resolved message states the incident start and end times with timezone, the affected scope, what was changed to fix it, and a dated commitment to a post-incident report. The post-incident customer email is sent by the deadline the matrix sets for that severity, and it links the report or summarises its corrective actions.

rationale.source: Google SRE book ch. 15 Postmortem Culture; Atlassian Incident Management Handbook

rule.rationale: "Resolved" with no window and no scope leaves every customer computing their own downtime for the SLA claim, and every account manager guessing. The dated postmortem commitment is the difference between a company that had an outage and a company that had an outage and will have it again.

rule.statement: Every variable in a template is a named token from the bundle's fixed list (for example `{{incident_id}}`, `{{impact}}`, `{{next_update_at}}`, `{{commander}}`). A filled instance MUST contain zero unresolved tokens and zero template comments before it is posted or sent; the validator rejects any instance that fails this check.

rationale.source: Widely established template-hygiene practice; this methodology's output contract

rule.rationale: A status page reading "We are investigating an issue affecting {{impact}}" has happened at companies that ship software for a living. It is the one comms failure that is fully preventable by a regex, and it is the one customers screenshot.

rule.statement: Each of the four templates carries a `last_drilled` date and is exercised in a game day or tabletop drill at least once per quarter and after any edit to the severity matrix, the status-page components, or the on-call rotation. A template whose `last_drilled` is older than 90 days is marked stale and cannot be the default for a live incident.

rationale.source: Google SRE book ch. 14 (practising incident management); PagerDuty Incident Response documentation

rule.rationale: Templates rot faster than services: the status-page component gets renamed, the exec distribution list loses the new COO, the commander rotation moves to a new tool. The drill is where a template referring to a retired component is found, instead of at minute 12 of a real P1.
